stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Collectors once prized each Edo-period woodblock print as the work of the single artist whose name appeared in its margin. Scholars now describe the prints' origins quite differently. Behind every sheet stood something far more collaborative______ a workshop in which a designer drew the image, a carver cut a separate block for each color, and a printer, working under a publisher who financed the edition, inked and pressed the paper by hand.
explanation: Start with the words before the blank. "Behind every sheet stood something far more collaborative" is a complete sentence, and it points forward to an unnamed "something." Now look at what comes after the blank. It contains three subject-verb pairs ("a designer drew," "a carver cut," "a printer . . . inked and pressed"), but all three sit inside the relative clause "in which . . .". That clause describes "a workshop." Remove it, along with the interrupter "working under a publisher who financed the edition," and only the noun phrase "a workshop" is left. So a complete clause is followed by a noun phrase that names what the clause promised, and a colon is the mark that introduces it.

B.why: You probably saw the verbs "drew," "cut," and "inked" and decided that the second part was a full clause. Each of those verbs belongs to the "in which" clause that modifies "a workshop," so the second part is only a noun phrase. A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides.

C.why: Adding "it was" does give the second part a subject and verb, but now there are two independent clauses joined by nothing more than a comma. That is a comma splice.

D.why: A period makes "A workshop in which . . . by hand" its own sentence. It has no main verb, because every verb in it belongs to the "in which" clause, so it is a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Seismometers are built to record earthquakes, so researchers reviewing global data in the late 1990s expected the instruments to fall silent between quakes. They did not. Even on the calmest days, the devices—sensitive enough to register a truck passing several kilometers away—picked up one signal they had never been designed to detect______ a faint, ceaseless vibration of the whole planet, which seismologists now attribute largely to ocean waves pressing on the seafloor.
explanation: First, cross out the dash-enclosed interrupter. That leaves "Even on the calmest days, the devices picked up one signal they had never been designed to detect." It is a complete sentence, and it ends by pointing to an unnamed "one signal." What follows the blank is the noun phrase "a faint, ceaseless vibration of the whole planet." The verb "attribute" belongs to the "which" clause that modifies that noun phrase, so it does not make the second part a full clause. A complete clause followed by a phrase that names what it promised takes a colon.

A.why: You may have taken "seismologists now attribute" as the second part's subject and verb. They belong to the "which" clause that describes "vibration," so what follows the blank is only a noun phrase. A semicolon needs an independent clause after it.

B.why: With "it was" added, the second part becomes an independent clause, and joining two independent clauses with only a comma is a comma splice.

D.why: A period makes "A faint, ceaseless vibration . . . seafloor" a sentence of its own. Its only verb sits inside the "which" clause, so the main noun phrase has no verb and the result is a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most nineteenth-century Japanese woodblock prints were made by a team: a designer drew the image, a carver cut it into cherry wood, and a printer inked and pressed each sheet. When conservators examined a set of 1830s landscape prints under raking light, they found traces of a fourth worker whom no record of the workshop mentions ______ burnisher whose thumb, pressed again and again into the damp paper, left faint whorls that survive today.
explanation: Ignore the opening "When..." clause and you have a complete sentence: "they found traces of a fourth worker whom no record of the workshop mentions." It ends by pointing to a worker it hasn't named yet. What follows names that worker, and it's only a noun phrase. "Whose thumb... left" and "that survive" are relative clauses describing the burnisher, not a main subject and verb. A complete clause followed by a phrase that identifies what it promised takes a colon.

A.why: You saw the verbs "left" and "survive" after the blank and decided the second half could stand alone. Both sit inside relative clauses, so "a burnisher whose thumb..." is a noun phrase, and a semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides.

B.why: Adding "it was" turns the second half into a complete sentence, and joining two complete sentences with only a comma makes a comma splice.

D.why: A period leaves "A burnisher whose thumb... left faint whorls that survive today" on its own as a sentence. Its verbs belong to relative clauses, so it has no main verb and is a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: An analysis of a seventeenth-century Dutch dyer's ledger shows that the workshop's celebrated "Leiden red" depended on far fewer ingredients than rival dyers assumed. Every batch recorded over three decades calls for the same short ______ madder root, alum from Liège, and the bran water in which the cloth was soaked overnight.
explanation: "Every batch recorded over three decades calls for the same short list" is a complete sentence that promises a list. What follows is that list, three noun phrases. The clause "in which the cloth was soaked" only describes the bran water. A colon after the complete clause introduces the list correctly.

B.why: You knew a list calls for a colon but put it in the wrong place. After "including" the clause isn't finished, because "including" needs its object, and a colon can't separate a word from its object.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides. The list after it has no main verb, and "was soaked" belongs to the relative clause about the bran water.

D.why: "These were madder root..." is a complete sentence, and joining it to another complete sentence with only a comma makes a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Early-twentieth-century researchers studying pellagra, a disease caused by a shortage of niacin, faced a puzzle. Poor communities in the American South that lived largely on corn were hit hard, yet in Mexico, where corn was eaten at nearly every meal, the disease was rare. The difference lay in a step that Mexican cooks had performed for ______ the kernels in limewater, a treatment that frees the niacin locked inside them.
explanation: "The difference lay in a step that Mexican cooks had performed for centuries" is complete, and it ends on a step it hasn't named yet. What follows names the step. It's a gerund phrase, "soaking the kernels in limewater," followed by an appositive. The only finite verb, "frees," sits inside the relative clause "that frees the niacin." A colon is the mark that delivers what the clause promised.

A.why: "They were soaking..." is a complete sentence, so a bare comma between it and the first clause makes a comma splice. "They" also has no clear referent.

B.why: "Soaking the kernels in limewater, a treatment that frees the niacin..." has no main verb, because "frees" belongs to the relative clause. A period leaves it standing as a fragment.

C.why: You read the verb "frees" as the main verb of a second clause and chose a semicolon because it looks formal. The words after the blank are a phrase, and a semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Buried beneath the plastered floor of one house at a Neolithic settlement in central Anatolia, directly under the spot where its occupants had kept their hearth, was something the excavators had not expected to ______ of obsidian blades, each wrapped in a strip of woven reed.
explanation: The sentence is inverted. Its subject is "something" and its verb is "was," so the part before the blank is a complete clause even though it opens with two long modifiers. "The excavators had not expected to find" describes "something," and "find" already has its object, "something." "A cache of obsidian blades" names that something, so it's a noun phrase explaining a complete clause, and a colon is the right mark.

A.why: "Expected to find a cache" sounds natural, but "find" already takes "something" as its object. Attaching "a cache" as a second object leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

C.why: You correctly spotted that the inverted opening is a complete clause, then reached for a semicolon. What follows is only a noun phrase, and a semicolon needs a complete clause after it too.

D.why: Adding "it was" makes the second half a complete sentence, and a bare comma between two complete sentences is a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Fossil leaves from an Eocene lakebed in Wyoming have given paleobotanists an unexpected record of ancient air. Each leaf preserves a feature that shifts with the air's carbon dioxide ______ density of stomata—the tiny pores through which a plant takes in gas—on its underside, a figure that falls as carbon dioxide rises.
explanation: "Each leaf preserves a feature that shifts with the air's carbon dioxide level" is complete, and the noun phrase after the blank names the feature. Normally a colon or a single dash would both work here. But the explanation already contains a pair of dashes around "the tiny pores through which a plant takes in gas." Only the colon introduces the explanation and leaves that pair intact.

A.why: You knew a single dash can work like a colon, but this dash would pair with the next one. That fences off "the density of stomata" as an interruption and leaves "the tiny pores...—on its underside" with nothing to attach to.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete clause after it. "The density of stomata... on its underside" is a noun phrase, and "takes" and "falls" sit inside relative clauses.

D.why: "It is the density..." is a complete sentence, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma makes a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When Paris was rebuilt in the 1850s and 1860s, its new boulevards owed their uniform look less to any single architect than to regulation. Owners on each boulevard could hire whomever they liked, but the buildings they put up were ______ held at a common height, so that a row of separately designed facades would read as one continuous wall.
choices: bound by: one rule in particular, a cornice line
bound by one rule in particular; a cornice line
bound by one rule in particular, it was a cornice line
bound by one rule in particular: a cornice line
explanation: The colon has to come after a complete clause. "The buildings they put up were bound by one rule in particular" is complete and points ahead to a rule it hasn't named. "A cornice line held at a common height..." names the rule, and it's a noun phrase. So the colon goes after "in particular."

A.why: You chose a colon but put it after "bound by," where the clause isn't finished. A colon can't separate a preposition from its object.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides. "A cornice line held at a common height" is a noun phrase, because "held" here is a participle, not a main verb.

C.why: "It was a cornice line..." is a complete sentence, and joining two complete sentences with only a comma makes a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Navigators searched the Atlantic west of Ireland for Isla Verdana for generations. The island, which mapmakers in Lisbon, Antwerp, and London copied from one another's charts for more than a century and which several captains swore they had glimpsed, had a mundane ______ copyist's misreading of a smudged depth sounding, a number he took for the outline of a coast.
explanation: Cross out the long interrupter that starts with "which mapmakers..." and you're left with "The island... had a mundane origin." That's a complete clause that promises an explanation. "A copyist's misreading of a smudged depth sounding" gives that explanation as a noun phrase. "He took" belongs to a relative clause describing "a number." A colon is correct.

B.why: With no punctuation, two noun phrases collide: "origin a copyist's misreading." The explanation needs a mark to introduce it.

C.why: You may have seen "he took" and read the second half as a complete clause. It's a noun phrase with a relative clause inside it, and a semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides.

D.why: "This was a copyist's misreading..." is a complete sentence, so joining it to the main clause with only a comma makes a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Over one season, a group of collegiate sprinters cut an average of 0.15 second from their 100-meter times, even though their weight-room numbers barely moved. The researchers traced the improvement to a variable that coaches rarely think to ______ contact time, the fraction of a second that each foot spends on the track during a stride.
explanation: "The researchers traced the improvement to a variable that coaches rarely think to measure" is complete. "Measure" already has its object, "that," which refers back to "variable." The clause names a variable without saying what it is, and "ground contact time..." answers that as a noun phrase with an appositive. A colon introduces it correctly.

A.why: "Think to measure ground contact time" reads smoothly, but "measure" already takes "that" as its object. Giving it a second object leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

C.why: You read the verb "spends" as the start of a second clause. It belongs to the relative clause "that each foot spends," so the second half is a noun phrase, and a semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides.

D.why: "It is ground contact time..." is a complete sentence, and joining two complete sentences with only a comma makes a comma splice.
